lines.text: A mountain land beneath Ararat, the first to make Christianity its faith, that has survived empires, genocide and war. This is the story of Armenia.
Nearly three thousand years ago, the kingdom of Urartu ruled the highlands around Lake Van, building fortresses and canals and standing up to Assyria.
In 782 BCE its king founded the fortress of Erebuni, which would grow into Yerevan, today's capital.
When Urartu fell, a Kingdom of Armenia took its place, and it would last for almost a thousand years.
Under Tigranes the Great, Armenia briefly became an empire reaching from the Caspian Sea to the Mediterranean.
Centuries later, Gregory the Illuminator converted King Tiridates, and around 301 Armenia became the first Christian nation.
Soon after, the cathedral of Etchmiadzin was built, the mother church of Armenia and one of the oldest in the world.
Around 405 the monk Mesrop Mashtots created the Armenian alphabet, so the people could read the Bible in their own tongue.
Persians, Arabs and Byzantines came and went. In the thirteenth century, monks carved Geghard monastery deep into a mountain gorge.
In 1903 Aram Khachaturian was born, the composer whose Sabre Dance would be heard around the world.
In 1915, during the First World War, the Ottoman government killed and deported the Armenians of Anatolia. Hundreds of thousands died, perhaps more than a million.
In 1918 a free Armenian republic was declared. Within a few years it fell to the Soviets.
In Paris in 1924, the son of Armenian refugees was born. Charles Aznavour became one of the great voices of French song.
In 1975 Nikol Pashinyan was born, the journalist who would one day lead the country.
In 1988, as Soviet power weakened, war broke out with Azerbaijan over Nagorno-Karabakh. Armenia won it in 1994.
That same year, an earthquake destroyed the town of Spitak and killed some twenty-five thousand people.
Armenia became independent in 1991. In 2018 peaceful protests swept the country and brought Pashinyan to power.
Two years later, in six weeks of war, Azerbaijan took back much of Karabakh.
And in September 2023, after a new offensive, nearly all the Armenians of Karabakh fled their homes.
Through every loss, Armenia has kept its faith, its alphabet and its name.
